subject: use Hapmap data as reference for affy 6.0 data

messages.author: 488c3d4a008f3eed
messages.subject: use Hapmap data as reference for affy 6.0 data
parts:
Hi,

I have some affymetrix SNP 6.0 data from tumor tissue to analyze. If I
choose to use the HapMap data set as reference (thetaR), should I do
normalization of my own data with the Hapmap data or I should
normalize them seperately?

For practical reason, I would like to be able to process the Hapmap
data once and get the rawCNs of them to use as reference whenever I
have new data come in.

Thanks,
Yupu

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] use Hapmap data as reference for affy 6.0 data
parts: Hi,

On Wed, Aug 27, 2008 at 10:48 AM, yupu <yupu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I have some affymetrix SNP 6.0 data from tumor tissue to analyze. If I
> choose to use the HapMap data set as reference (thetaR), should I do
> normalization of my own data with the Hapmap data or I should
> normalize them seperately?

this is a tricky question and I do not know of any published studies
that assess the performances of different approach. However, I'll try
to share some of my experience on this. A few years ago I was asked
to process 3(!) 500K arrays and turned to the public HapMap data as a
"gold standard" reference. I pooled the samples of interest with the
HapMap samples and batch processed them all together. At the time, I
think it was a quantile normalization and summarization via the
log-additive model. There were some interesting regions but tons of
"maybes". When the lab later got more samples processed I dropped the
HapMap samples and just used the in-house samples. Already at 10-15
arrays I saw an improvement compared to pooling it with 270 HapMap
samples. It should be noted that the samples studied were tumor
samples as well, but we still got much better signal. Of course, in
the downstream analysis we later had to carefully validate the regions
and make sure we didn't miss any because all samples had the same
regions etc. Anyway, take home message is to use in-house samples,
if possible.

>
> For practical reason, I would like to be able to process the Hapmap
> data once and get the rawCNs of them to use as reference whenever I
> have new data come in.

The easiest is to pool them all together and rerun the batch. You can
do this once in a while, say over the weekend. If you look at the
CRMA method, you'll find that the allelic crosstalk calibration is
single-array by nature, so that one does not have to be rerun. So is
the AvgPlm summarization in theory, but due to the current
implementation you actually have to run all samples together.
(Details: That is just because I reused all the code from the
multi-array RmaPlm method to get something that works, and due to time
I haven't had time to revisit this). So, if I just find the time to
update AvgPlm, nothing has to be rerun here either. The following
fragment-length normalization is normalizing toward a target function,
which is the pooled average of all arrays. So here you need a
reference/all data. There is actual code prepared to allow you to
specify the reference in this step, but for reason explained below, it
is not worth spending energy on this approach right now.

If you can wait a bit, I've got good news though: I am
writing/finishing up the paper for our new CRMA v2 method and when
that is submitted and we get positive feedback from the reviewers, we
will post this new method (a vignette and updated code) online asap.
This new method is in theory a fully single-array method all the way
through that will provide you with chip effect estimates that are
better than what the current CRMA (v1) produces. With that method in
place, you won't have to worry about including HapMap or not in the
pre-processing; you will get identical chip-effect estimates in either
case. Thus, CRMA v2 "procrastinates" the decision to use a
gold-standard reference or not to a later step in the pipeline
(genotyping, CN/LOH calling etc).

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.author: 67dd8164f9bfa181
messages.subject: Re: use Hapmap data as reference for affy 6.0 data
parts:
I can support Henrik's observation regarding the HapMap samples. In
the 500k setting, 25 HapMap produce more noise when used as reference
compared to our in-house data (comparable number; non-cancer samples).
When doing small pilot series of cancer samples in the 6.0 setting, we
needed a normal reference set. Again, HapMap did not lead to good
results (though here we still have to do in-house reference samples
for comparison).

Henrik: We all will appreciate a commented R batch, for a situation as
the one described above, showing your preferred way to do it ;-)

Michael Baudis.

Dear All,

along a similar line I have the following question.

The standard for aroma.affymetrix (and other software) is to use as
reference the robust average across the sample.
I wonder if there is a rule of the thumb for how many arrays make a
good reference?

In the vignette 6 arrays are used. I guess this should be considered
enough?
Adding more arrays should in general improve the results?

In the specific case I have 6 arrays from stem cells to use for CN,
and I have also 20 arrays from another experiment (blod from healthy
people)
that I could add to get a more stable baseline. Would this be
reccomended?

Cheers

Marco

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: use Hapmap data as reference for affy 6.0 data
parts: Hi.

On Thu, Sep 18, 2008 at 5:10 AM, marco <mazu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear All,
>
> along a similar line I have the following question.
>
> The standard for aroma.affymetrix (and other software) is to use as
> reference the robust average across the sample.
> I wonder if there is a rule of the thumb for how many arrays make a
> good reference?

I'd say with 15-25 in-house arrays you do better than any number (I
tried 270) HapMap samples.

>
> In the vignette 6 arrays are used. I guess this should be considered
> enough?

Nope. The examples are using 6 arrays so they are relatively fast to
process. You should definitely aim for more if you want to use a
pooled reference.
> Adding more arrays should in general improve the results?

Yes. Discussion the reference here, the noise level of the pooled
reference goes down. With twice as many arrays, the average/mean
array will have half the variance, that is, with four times the number
of arrays the standard deviation of the mean goes down to half.

The variance of the test arrays will eventually be much greater than
the variance of the average array. Then adding more arrays to the
reference will not make much differences.

>
> In the specific case I have 6 arrays from stem cells to use for CN,
> and I have also 20 arrays from another experiment (blod from healthy
> people)
> that I could add to get a more stable baseline. Would this be
> reccomended?

I think so, especially if they were processed at the same microarray
facility and even more so if they were done close in time. Try with
and without and search for a deletion/amplification that you can spot
by eye. I would expect that you will see a much cleaner aberration
with the extra 20 arrays.

Cheers

Henrik
